goals: Compare ammonotelism, ureotelism and uricotelism with examples

slides.heading: Excretory Products and their Elimination
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why animals must remove nitrogenous wastes, and the structures that do it.

visual.alt: Flow from the breakdown of proteins to ammonia, urea and uric acid

slides.narration: Animals accumulate ammonia, urea, uric acid, carbon dioxide, water and ions such as sodium, potassium and chloride through metabolism or excess intake. These must be removed totally or partially. Ammonia, urea and uric acid are the major forms of nitrogenous wastes.

slides.heading: Three ways to get rid of nitrogen
slides.body_md: The choice of nitrogenous waste depends largely on how much **water** the animal can spare.

rows: Most toxic; needs a large amount of water
Many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects
Less toxic; made from ammonia in the liver
Mammals, many terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes
Least toxic; removed as pellet or paste with minimum loss of water

visual.alt: Table comparing ammonia, urea and uric acid excretion with examples

slides.narration: Ammonia is the most toxic and needs plenty of water, so ammonotelic animals live in water; ammonia, being very soluble, diffuses out across the body surface or the gills as ammonium ions. Land animals make less toxic urea in the liver. Reptiles, birds, land snails and insects save the most water by excreting uric acid as a pellet or paste.

slides.heading: Quick check: least toxic waste
slides.body_md: Which waste can be removed with the least loss of water?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the pellet or paste of birds and lizards.

slides.heading: Excretory structures in animals
slides.body_md: Most invertebrates have simple tubular excretory structures; vertebrates have complex tubular organs called **kidneys**.

rows: Flatworms such as Planaria, rotifers, some annelids, Amphioxus
Remove nitrogenous wastes; fluid and ionic balance

visual.alt: Table of excretory structures in animals

slides.narration: Flame cells of flatworms mainly control ionic and fluid volume. Earthworm nephridia remove wastes and keep fluid and ionic balance. Insects use Malpighian tubules, and prawns use antennal glands, also called green glands.

slides.heading: The human excretory system
slides.body_md: A pair of **kidneys**, one pair of **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and a **urethra**.

slides.narration: The kidneys are reddish brown, bean shaped organs between the levels of the last thoracic and the third lumbar vertebra, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity. Each receives a renal artery and drains into a renal vein. Urine flows down the ureters to the bladder and leaves through the urethra.

slides.heading: The kidney in numbers
slides.body_md: Each adult kidney is roughly the size of a fist-sized bar of soap.

rows: nearly one million in each kidney

visual.alt: Table of the size, mass and nephron number of a human kidney

slides.narration: A kidney is ten to twelve centimetres long, five to seven wide and two to three thick, and weighs about one hundred and twenty to one hundred and seventy grams. Each contains nearly a million nephrons, its functional units.

slides.heading: Inside the kidney
slides.body_md: A notch on the inner concave surface, the **hilum**, lets in the ureter, blood vessels and nerves. Inner to it lies the funnel-shaped **renal pelvis** with projections called **calyces**.

slides.body_md: Each nephron has a **glomerulus** and a **renal tubule**. The glomerulus and **Bowman’s capsule** together form the **Malpighian body** (renal corpuscle).

slides.narration: The afferent arteriole, a fine branch of the renal artery, forms the glomerulus, and the efferent arteriole carries blood away. The tubule runs from Bowman’s capsule as the coiled proximal convoluted tubule, the hairpin Henle’s loop, and the distal convoluted tubule, which opens into a collecting duct. The efferent arteriole forms peritubular capillaries, and a U shaped vessel beside the loop, the vasa recta.

slides.heading: Cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons
slides.body_md: The Malpighian body, PCT and DCT lie in the **cortex**; Henle’s loop dips into the **medulla**.

rows: Too short; extends very little into the medulla
Very long; runs deep into the medulla

visual.alt: Table comparing cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons

slides.narration: Most nephrons are cortical, with short loops. A few, the juxtamedullary nephrons, have very long loops that run deep into the medulla alongside the vasa recta. These long loops matter for making concentrated urine.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which waste suits which animal?
slides.body_md: Predict the main nitrogenous waste of each animal and give the reason.
bullets: A rohu fish in a river → **ammonia**: plenty of water to carry it away across the gills.
A camel in a desert → **urea**: a mammal, so ureotelic; urea is less toxic than ammonia.
A garden lizard → **uric acid**: excreted as a paste with minimum loss of water.
A cockroach → **uric acid**, removed by its **Malpighian tubules**.

visual.alt: Worked table matching four animals with their nitrogenous wastes

slides.narration: Ask how much water the animal can afford to lose. Fish can flush toxic ammonia away. Mammals convert it to urea. Reptiles and insects, which must save water, excrete almost dry uric acid.

slides.heading: Step 1 of urine formation: glomerular filtration
slides.body_md: Glomerular capillary **blood pressure** forces fluid through three layers: the **endothelium** of the glomerular vessels, the **epithelium of Bowman’s capsule** (podocytes with **filtration slits**) and a **basement membrane** between them. Almost all plasma constituents **except proteins** pass: this is **ultrafiltration**.

nodes.label: Endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes with slit pores

visual.alt: Flow of glomerular filtration through three layers into Bowman’s capsule

slides.narration: About eleven to twelve hundred millilitres of blood pass through the kidneys every minute, roughly one fifth of what each ventricle pumps. The amount of filtrate formed per minute is the glomerular filtration rate, about one hundred and twenty five millilitres a minute in a healthy person.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from GFR to litres per day
slides.body_md: The GFR of a healthy adult is about 125 mL per minute. How much filtrate is formed in a day? About what share of a cardiac output of 5000 mL per minute is the renal blood flow of 1100 mL per minute?
bullets: Minutes in a day: $24 \times 60 = 1440$.
Filtrate: $125 \times 1440 = 180000$ mL, that is 180 litres a day.
Renal share: $\dfrac{1100}{5000} \times 100 = 22$ percent, roughly one fifth.

visual.alt: Worked table: 180 litres of filtrate a day; renal blood flow about 22 percent of cardiac output

slides.narration: One hundred and twenty five millilitres every minute, over fourteen hundred and forty minutes, makes one hundred and eighty thousand millilitres, or one hundred and eighty litres of filtrate each day. Yet we pass only a litre or so of urine, so almost all of it must be reabsorbed.

slides.body_md: What is the glomerular filtration rate of a healthy adult?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the volume filtered each minute.

bullets: Ammonia (ammonotelic, aquatic), urea (ureotelic, made in the liver), uric acid (uricotelic, saves water).
Protonephridia (Planaria), nephridia (earthworm), Malpighian tubules (insects), antennal glands (prawn).
Kidneys 10–12 cm long, 120–170 g; capsule, cortex, medullary pyramids, columns of Bertini, calyces, pelvis, hilum.

Ultrafiltration through three layers; GFR about 125 mL per minute, 180 L per day.

decks.title: Excretory Products and their Elimination — Part 2: Reabsorption, concentration, regulation and disorders
goals: Explain reabsorption and secretion and the roles of each segment of the tubule
Explain the counter-current mechanism that concentrates urine
Describe regulation by ADH, the renin–angiotensin mechanism and ANF
Describe micturition, the role of other organs, and kidney disorders with their treatment

slides.heading: Making urine
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how the filtrate is turned into urine, how the body controls it, and what happens when kidneys fail.

visual.alt: Flow of the three processes of urine formation

slides.narration: Urine formation involves three processes: glomerular filtration, reabsorption and secretion. Filtration gives a large volume of filtrate. The tubules then take back almost all of it and add a few substances, leaving a small volume of urine.

slides.heading: Reabsorption and secretion
slides.body_md: Nearly **99 percent** of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the tubules, by **active** or **passive** mechanisms.

rows: Nitrogenous wastes; water in the initial segments
Hydrogen ions, potassium ions and ammonia added to the filtrate; keeps ionic and acid–base balance

visual.alt: Table of active and passive reabsorption and tubular secretion

slides.narration: The tubular cells pump back valuable substances such as glucose, amino acids and sodium. Water and some wastes follow passively. At the same time the cells secrete hydrogen ions, potassium ions and ammonia into the filtrate, which keeps the ionic and acid base balance of the body fluids.

slides.heading: What each segment does
slides.body_md: Different parts of the tubule have different jobs.

rows: Brush border epithelium; reabsorbs nearly all nutrients and 70–80 percent of electrolytes and water; secretes hydrogen ions, ammonia and potassium ions; absorbs bicarbonate
Permeable to water, almost impermeable to electrolytes: filtrate becomes concentrated
Impermeable to water, transports electrolytes out: filtrate becomes dilute
Conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water; reabsorbs bicarbonate; secretes hydrogen and potassium ions and ammonia
Large amounts of water reabsorbed for concentrated urine; lets some urea into the medulla; secretes hydrogen and potassium ions

visual.alt: Table of the roles of the segments of the renal tubule

slides.narration: The proximal tubule does most of the reabsorbing. The two limbs of Henle’s loop behave oppositely: the descending limb lets water out, the ascending limb lets salts out. The distal tubule fine tunes sodium, water and acid base balance, and the collecting duct can reabsorb large amounts of water to make concentrated urine.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much is reabsorbed?
slides.body_md: A person forms 180 L of filtrate and passes 1.5 L of urine in a day. How much filtrate is reabsorbed, and what percentage is that? How much of it is taken back in the PCT if that segment handles 70–80 percent?
bullets: Percentage: $\dfrac{178.5}{180} \times 100 \approx 99.17$ percent, nearly 99 percent.

visual.alt: Worked table: 178.5 litres, about 99.17 percent, reabsorbed

slides.narration: Take the urine away from the filtrate to get one hundred and seventy eight point five litres reabsorbed, a little over ninety nine percent. Seventy to eighty percent of the filtrate, one hundred and twenty six to one hundred and forty four litres, is taken back in the proximal tubule alone.

slides.heading: Concentrating urine: the counter-current mechanism
slides.body_md: Filtrate flows in **opposite directions** in the two limbs of Henle’s loop, and blood does the same in the two limbs of the **vasa recta**: two **counter-currents**. They keep the osmolarity of the medullary interstitium rising from about **300** in the cortex to about **1200 mOsmol per L** in the inner medulla.

slides.narration: The gradient is mainly due to sodium chloride and urea. Sodium chloride leaves the ascending limb, is picked up by the descending vasa recta and returned to the interstitium by the ascending vasa recta. Small amounts of urea leave the collecting duct, enter the thin ascending limb and are carried back. This counter current mechanism maintains the gradient.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how concentrated can urine be?
slides.body_md: The filtrate entering the tubule has about the osmolarity of plasma, 300 mOsmol per L. The inner medulla reaches about 1200. How many times more concentrated than the filtrate can the urine become, and why?
bullets: As the collecting duct passes through ever saltier medulla, **water leaves it** into the interstitium.
Human kidneys can make urine **nearly four times** as concentrated as the initial filtrate.

visual.alt: Worked table: osmolarity rising 300, 600, 900, 1200

slides.narration: Twelve hundred divided by three hundred is four. Water can leave the collecting duct only while the fluid outside is more concentrated, so the deepest medulla sets the limit: urine nearly four times as concentrated as the filtrate.

slides.heading: Regulation by ADH
slides.body_md: Kidney function is monitored and regulated by **hormonal feedback** involving the **hypothalamus**, the **JGA** and, to some extent, the **heart**.

nodes.label: More water reabsorbed from the later parts of the tubule

visual.alt: Flow of the ADH feedback that conserves water

slides.narration: Osmoreceptors respond to changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration. When the body loses too much fluid, the hypothalamus releases antidiuretic hormone from the neurohypophysis, and more water is reabsorbed. When fluid volume rises, the receptors switch off and less hormone is released. The hormone also constricts blood vessels, raising blood pressure and the filtration rate.

slides.heading: The renin–angiotensin mechanism and ANF
slides.body_md: A fall in glomerular blood flow, pressure or GFR activates the **JG cells** to release **renin**.

nodes.label: Vasoconstriction: glomerular pressure and GFR rise
Aldosterone from adrenal cortex: sodium ions and water reabsorbed

visual.alt: Flow of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone mechanism

slides.narration: Angiotensin two is a powerful vasoconstrictor, so it raises glomerular blood pressure and the filtration rate. It also makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone, which increases reabsorption of sodium and water from the distal parts of the tubule. When more blood flows into the atria, the heart releases atrial natriuretic factor, which dilates vessels and lowers blood pressure, acting as a check on this mechanism.

slides.heading: Quick check: ADH
slides.body_md: Predict the hormone response described.
slides.narration: Quick check. Does losing water raise or lower the release of antidiuretic hormone?

slides.heading: Micturition
slides.body_md: Urine is stored in the **urinary bladder** until the **CNS** gives a voluntary signal.

nodes.label: Motor messages: bladder smooth muscle contracts, urethral sphincter relaxes

visual.alt: Flow of the micturition reflex

slides.narration: Releasing urine is called micturition, and the neural mechanism behind it is the micturition reflex. An adult passes on average one to one and a half litres of urine a day, a light yellow, slightly acidic fluid with about twenty five to thirty grams of urea.

slides.heading: Other organs that help in excretion
slides.body_md: The **lungs, liver and skin** also remove wastes.

rows: Large amounts of carbon dioxide (about 200 mL per minute) and water
Bile with bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs
Sweat with NaCl, small amounts of urea and lactic acid
Sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes in sebum

visual.alt: Table of the excretory roles of the lungs, liver, skin and saliva

slides.narration: Most of what the liver puts into bile leaves with the digestive wastes. Sweat mainly cools the body surface, but it also removes some wastes. Sebum forms a protective oily covering for the skin. Urine tests help doctors: glucose and ketone bodies in urine point to diabetes mellitus.

slides.heading: Disorders of the excretory system
slides.body_md: Malfunctioning kidneys let **urea accumulate in the blood** (**uraemia**), which can lead to **kidney failure**.

rows: Blood with heparin is passed through a cellophane tube in dialysing fluid that lacks nitrogenous wastes; wastes diffuse out; anti-heparin added before return
Ultimate correction of acute renal failure; donor preferably a close relative to reduce rejection
Stones of crystallised salts, such as oxalates, formed in the kidney
Inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney

slides.narration: In haemodialysis, blood from an artery is mixed with an anticoagulant such as heparin and pumped through a coiled cellophane tube bathed in fluid like plasma but without nitrogenous wastes. notes.title: Excretory Products and their Elimination — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Modes of excretion and the human excretory system
sections.body_md:
Animals accumulate ammonia, urea, uric acid, carbon dioxide, water and ions such as sodium, potassium, chloride, phosphate and sulphate, through metabolism or excess ingestion; these must be removed totally or partially. **Ammonia, urea and uric acid** are the major forms of nitrogenous wastes.

- **Ammonotelism** (excreting ammonia): ammonia is the **most toxic** and needs a **large amount of water** for elimination. Many **bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects** are ammonotelic. Being readily soluble, ammonia is generally excreted by **diffusion across body surfaces or through the gill surfaces** (in fish) as ammonium ions; the kidneys play no significant role.
- **Ureotelism** (excreting urea): **mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes**. Ammonia produced by metabolism is converted into **urea in the liver**, released into the blood, filtered and excreted by the kidneys. Some urea may be retained in the kidney matrix of some animals to maintain a desired osmolarity.
- **Uricotelism** (excreting uric acid): **reptiles, birds, land snails and insects** excrete nitrogenous wastes as **uric acid** in the form of a **pellet or paste**, with a **minimum loss of water**. Uric acid is the least toxic.

**Excretory structures.** Most invertebrates have simple tubular forms; vertebrates have complex tubular organs, the kidneys.
- **Protonephridia or flame cells:** Platyhelminthes (flatworms such as *Planaria*), rotifers, some annelids and the cephalochordate *Amphioxus*; mainly **osmoregulation** (ionic and fluid volume regulation).
- **Nephridia:** earthworms and other annelids; remove nitrogenous wastes and maintain fluid and ionic balance.
- **Malpighian tubules:** most insects, including cockroaches; remove nitrogenous wastes and help osmoregulation.
- **Antennal glands or green glands:** crustaceans such as prawns.

**Human excretory system:** a pair of **kidneys**, one pair of **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and a **urethra**. The kidneys are reddish brown, bean-shaped and lie between the levels of the **last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra**, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity. Each adult kidney is **10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide and 2–3 cm thick**, weighing **120–170 g** on average (sizes vary between people). Towards the centre of the inner concave surface is a notch, the **hilum**, through which the ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter. Inner to the hilum is the broad funnel-shaped **renal pelvis** with projections called **calyces**. The outer layer is a tough **capsule**. Inside are an outer **cortex** and an inner **medulla**; the medulla is divided into a few conical **medullary pyramids** projecting into the calyces, and the cortex extends between them as renal columns, the **columns of Bertini**.

**Nephron.** Each kidney has nearly **one million** nephrons, the functional units. Each has a **glomerulus** and a **renal tubule**. The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries formed by the **afferent arteriole**, a fine branch of the renal artery; blood leaves by the **efferent arteriole**. The tubule begins as a double-walled cup, **Bowman’s capsule**, which encloses the glomerulus; together they form the **Malpighian body (renal corpuscle)**. Next come the highly coiled **proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)**, the hairpin-shaped **Henle’s loop** (descending and ascending limbs) and the coiled **distal convoluted tubule (DCT)**. The DCTs of many nephrons open into a straight **collecting duct**; collecting ducts converge and open into the renal pelvis through the medullary pyramids in the calyces. The Malpighian corpuscle, PCT and DCT lie in the **cortex**; the loop of Henle dips into the **medulla**. In most nephrons the loop is short and extends very little into the medulla (**cortical nephrons**); in some it is very long and runs deep into the medulla (**juxtamedullary nephrons**). The efferent arteriole forms **peritubular capillaries** around the tubule; a minute vessel of this network runs parallel to Henle’s loop as the U-shaped **vasa recta**, which is absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons.

sections.heading: 2. Urine formation and regulation of kidney function
sections.body_md:
Urine formation involves **glomerular filtration, reabsorption and secretion**, in different parts of the nephron.

**Glomerular filtration.** On average **1100–1200 mL of blood** are filtered by the kidneys per minute, roughly one-fifth of the blood pumped by each ventricle in a minute. Glomerular capillary blood pressure filters blood through three layers: the **endothelium** of the glomerular vessels, the **epithelium of Bowman’s capsule** and a **basement membrane** between them. The epithelial cells of Bowman’s capsule, **podocytes**, leave minute spaces called **filtration slits or slit pores**. Almost all plasma constituents **except proteins** pass into Bowman’s capsule: **ultrafiltration**. The **glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** of a healthy person is about **125 mL per minute**, that is **180 litres per day**.

The **juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)** is a sensitive region formed by cellular modifications in the DCT and the afferent arteriole where they touch. A fall in GFR activates the **JG cells** to release **renin**, which can bring glomerular blood flow, and so the GFR, back to normal.

**Reabsorption.** Nearly **99 percent** of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the tubules, by active or passive mechanisms: glucose, amino acids and sodium ions **actively**; nitrogenous wastes **passively**; water passively in the initial segments.

**Secretion.** Tubular cells secrete **hydrogen ions, potassium ions and ammonia** into the filtrate, helping to maintain the **ionic and acid–base balance** of body fluids.

**Roles of the segments.**
- **PCT:** simple cuboidal **brush border** epithelium increases the surface for reabsorption; nearly all essential nutrients and **70–80 percent of electrolytes and water** are reabsorbed here. It keeps pH and ionic balance by selectively secreting hydrogen ions, ammonia and potassium ions and absorbing bicarbonate.
- **Henle’s loop:** reabsorption is minimal in the ascending limb; the loop maintains the **high osmolarity of the medullary interstitial fluid**. The **descending limb** is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, so the filtrate becomes **concentrated** as it moves down. The **ascending limb** is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes actively or passively, so the filtrate becomes **dilute** as it moves up.
- **DCT:** conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water; reabsorbs bicarbonate and selectively secretes hydrogen and potassium ions and ammonia, keeping pH and sodium–potassium balance.
- **Collecting duct:** runs from the cortex to the inner medulla; large amounts of water can be reabsorbed here to make **concentrated urine**; lets small amounts of **urea** into the medullary interstitium to keep up its osmolarity; secretes hydrogen and potassium ions.

**Counter-current mechanism.** Mammals can produce concentrated urine; Henle’s loop and the vasa recta are essential. Filtrate flows in **opposite directions** in the two limbs of Henle’s loop, a **counter-current**, and blood flows in a counter-current in the two limbs of the vasa recta. Their closeness and the counter-currents maintain an **osmolarity that increases towards the inner medulla, from 300 mOsmol per L in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmol per L in the inner medulla**. The gradient is mainly caused by **NaCl and urea**. NaCl transported by the ascending limb of Henle’s loop is exchanged with the descending limb of the vasa recta and returned to the interstitium by its ascending portion. Small amounts of urea enter the thin segment of the ascending limb and are transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule. The gradient allows easy passage of **water from the collecting tubule**, concentrating the filtrate; human kidneys can produce urine **nearly four times** as concentrated as the initial filtrate.

**Regulation** involves hormonal feedback through the **hypothalamus, the JGA and, to some extent, the heart**.
- **ADH:** osmoreceptors respond to changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration. An excessive loss of fluid stimulates the hypothalamus to release **antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin)** from the **neurohypophysis**; ADH increases water reabsorption from the later parts of the tubule, **preventing diuresis**. A rise in body fluid volume switches the receptors off and suppresses ADH release. ADH also constricts blood vessels, raising blood pressure and so glomerular blood flow and GFR.
- **Renin–angiotensin mechanism:** a fall in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure or GFR activates the JG cells to release **renin**, which converts **angiotensinogen** to **angiotensin I** and further to **angiotensin II**. Angiotensin II, a powerful **vasoconstrictor**, raises glomerular blood pressure and GFR; it also makes the **adrenal cortex** release **aldosterone**, which increases reabsorption of **sodium ions and water** from the distal parts of the tubule, raising blood pressure and GFR.
- **ANF:** increased blood flow to the atria of the heart causes release of **atrial natriuretic factor**, which causes **vasodilation** and lowers blood pressure; it acts as a **check on the renin–angiotensin mechanism**.

sections.heading: 3. Micturition, role of other organs and disorders
sections.body_md:
**Micturition.** Urine formed by the nephrons is carried to the **urinary bladder** and stored until a voluntary signal comes from the **CNS**. As the bladder fills and stretches, **stretch receptors** in its wall send signals to the CNS; the CNS sends motor messages that make the **smooth muscles of the bladder contract** and the **urethral sphincter relax**, releasing urine. The process is **micturition**, and the neural mechanism causing it is the **micturition reflex**.

**Urine.** An adult excretes on average **1 to 1.5 litres** of urine per day: a light yellow, watery, slightly acidic fluid (**pH about 6.0**) with a characteristic odour. On average **25–30 g of urea** is excreted per day. Urine analysis helps diagnose many metabolic disorders and kidney malfunctions; for example, **glucose (glycosuria)** and **ketone bodies (ketonuria)** in urine indicate **diabetes mellitus**. (Daily volumes depend on water intake and climate.)

**Other organs.**
- **Lungs** remove large amounts of carbon dioxide (about **200 mL per minute**) and significant quantities of water every day.
- **Liver**, the largest gland, secretes **bile** containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs; most of these pass out with the digestive wastes.
- **Skin:** **sweat glands** produce sweat, a watery fluid with NaCl, small amounts of urea, lactic acid and so on; its main role is to cool the body surface, but it also removes some wastes. **Sebaceous glands** eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through **sebum**, which gives a protective oily covering to the skin.
- **Saliva** can eliminate small amounts of nitrogenous wastes.

**Disorders.**
- Malfunctioning kidneys lead to accumulation of urea in the blood, **uraemia**, which is highly harmful and may lead to **kidney failure**.
- **Haemodialysis:** blood drained from a convenient artery is pumped into a dialysing unit after adding an **anticoagulant such as heparin**. The unit has a coiled **cellophane tube** surrounded by **dialysing fluid** with the same composition as plasma **except the nitrogenous wastes**. The porous membrane lets molecules pass along their concentration gradient, so the wastes move out of the blood. The cleared blood is pumped back through a vein after adding **anti-heparin**. Thousands of uraemic patients have been helped by this method.
- **Kidney transplantation** is the ultimate method of correcting acute renal failure. A functioning kidney from a donor, preferably a **close relative**, is used to minimise the chance of **rejection by the immune system** of the host. Modern clinical procedures have increased the success rate.
- **Renal calculi:** stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts (oxalates and others) formed within the kidney.
- **Glomerulonephritis:** inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying ammonia is least toxic (it is the most toxic; uric acid is the least).
- Calling Malpighian tubules the excretory organs of earthworms (earthworms have nephridia; insects have Malpighian tubules).
- Writing that plasma proteins enter the filtrate (ultrafiltration holds back proteins).
- Swapping the permeability of the two limbs of Henle’s loop.
- Writing that ADH comes from the adrenal gland (it is released from the neurohypophysis on a signal from the hypothalamus).
- Saying ANF raises blood pressure (it causes vasodilation and lowers it).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a mode of excretion with an example, a kidney part, a tubule segment, a hormone and its source, a disorder.
- 2–3-mark answers: modes of excretion; kidney section; nephron; filtration and the JGA; roles of tubule segments; ADH and renin–angiotensin; micturition; other organs; dialysis.
- 5-mark answers: the human excretory system with the nephron; urine formation; the counter-current mechanism and regulation; disorders and their treatment.
- Numericals: GFR to litres per day, percentage reabsorbed, concentration factor — show the working.

answer.model_answer_md: Under a tough **capsule** lie an outer **cortex** and an inner **medulla**. questions.stem_md: Compare ammonotelism, ureotelism and uricotelism, giving the waste, its toxicity and two animal examples of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Ammonotelism:** waste **ammonia**, the **most toxic**, needing much water; many **bony fishes** and **aquatic amphibians** (also aquatic insects).

**Ureotelism:** waste **urea**, less toxic, made from ammonia in the **liver**; **mammals** and many **terrestrial amphibians** (also marine fishes).

**Uricotelism:** waste **uric acid**, the **least toxic**, removed as a pellet or paste with **minimum water loss**; **reptiles** and **birds** (also land snails and insects).

questions.solution_md: Three modes with wastes and examples.

questions.stem_md: Name the parts of a nephron in the order in which the filtrate passes through them, and state which parts lie in the cortex and which dip into the medulla.

answer.model_answer_md: Filtrate forms in **Bowman’s capsule** around the **glomerulus** (together the Malpighian body), then flows through the **proximal convoluted tubule**, the **descending and ascending limbs of Henle’s loop**, the **distal convoluted tubule** and into a **collecting duct**. The Malpighian body, PCT and DCT lie in the **cortex**; **Henle’s loop** dips into the **medulla**, and the collecting duct runs through it to the pelvis.

questions.solution_md: Order of parts; cortex and medulla.

questions.stem_md: Describe the human excretory system. Give the position, size and internal structure of a kidney, and describe the structure of a nephron with its blood supply.

answer.model_answer_md:
**System.** A pair of kidneys, one pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.

**Kidney.** The reddish brown, bean-shaped kidneys lie between the levels of the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity. Each is about 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide and 2–3 cm thick and weighs 120–170 g. A notch, the hilum, on the inner concave surface admits the ureter, vessels and nerves; inner to it is the renal pelvis with calyces. Under a tough capsule are the outer cortex and inner medulla; the medulla forms medullary pyramids projecting into the calyces, and the cortex extends between them as columns of Bertini.

**Nephron.** Each kidney has nearly one million nephrons. The afferent arteriole, a branch of the renal artery, forms the glomerulus, enclosed by the double-walled Bowman’s capsule; together they are the Malpighian body. The tubule continues as the coiled PCT, the hairpin Henle’s loop with descending and ascending limbs, and the coiled DCT, which opens into a collecting duct leading to the pelvis. The efferent arteriole leaves the glomerulus and forms peritubular capillaries; a minute vessel running parallel to Henle’s loop forms the U-shaped vasa recta. Most nephrons are cortical, with short loops and little or no vasa recta; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops deep in the medulla.

questions.solution_md: System, kidney, nephron with blood supply.

questions.stem_md: A museum display asks: “Why do a goldfish, a cat and a sparrow get rid of nitrogen in different chemical forms?” Write the explanation for the display, and add the excretory structures used by invertebrates such as flatworms, earthworms, insects and prawns.

answer.model_answer_md:
**The problem.** Breaking down proteins and nucleic acids produces ammonia, which must be removed. The form an animal excretes depends mainly on how much water it can spare.

**Goldfish: ammonia.** Ammonia is the most toxic waste and needs a large amount of water. A fish lives in water, so the readily soluble ammonia simply diffuses out across the body surface and gills as ammonium ions. This is ammonotelism, also seen in aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects.

**Cat: urea.** A land mammal cannot spend so much water. Its liver converts ammonia into less toxic urea, which is released into the blood and removed by the kidneys. This is ureotelism, shared by many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes.

**Sparrow: uric acid.** Birds, like reptiles, land snails and insects, must save as much water as possible. They excrete uric acid, the least toxic form, as a pellet or paste with minimum loss of water: uricotelism.

**Invertebrates.** Flatworms such as Planaria use protonephridia or flame cells, mainly for osmoregulation; earthworms use nephridia; insects such as cockroaches use Malpighian tubules; and crustaceans such as prawns use antennal or green glands.

questions.solution_md: Three modes linked to water; invertebrate structures.

marking_scheme.step: Link between waste and water availability

options.text_md: impermeable to water but permeable to electrolytes
impermeable to both water and electrolytes

the main site of glucose reabsorption

Large amounts of urea are secreted into the limb from the vasa recta.

The adrenal cortex releases more aldosterone.

The neurohypophysis releases more ADH.

Stops filtration in the glomerulus

questions.stem_md: Explain what makes glomerular filtration an ultrafiltration, naming the layers through which blood is filtered.

answer.model_answer_md: Glomerular **blood pressure** forces fluid through three layers: the **endothelium** of the glomerular capillaries, a **basement membrane**, and the **epithelium of Bowman’s capsule**, whose **podocytes** leave **filtration slits**. The filter is so fine that almost everything in plasma passes **except the proteins**: hence ultrafiltration.

questions.solution_md: Three layers; proteins held back.

marking_scheme.step: Blood pressure and the three layers

questions.stem_md: What is the juxtaglomerular apparatus, and how does it help when the GFR falls?

answer.model_answer_md: The **JGA** is a sensitive region formed by **cellular modifications in the DCT and the afferent arteriole** where they touch. When GFR falls, its **JG cells release renin**, which starts the renin–angiotensin mechanism, raising glomerular blood flow and pressure and bringing the **GFR back to normal**.

questions.solution_md: Structure and renin.

marking_scheme.step: DCT and afferent arteriole at contact

questions.stem_md: A person loses a lot of blood in an accident and his glomerular blood pressure falls. Outline the renin–angiotensin response that helps restore his GFR.

answer.model_answer_md: JG cells release **renin**, which converts **angiotensinogen** to **angiotensin I** and then **angiotensin II**. Angiotensin II, a powerful **vasoconstrictor**, raises **glomerular blood pressure** and GFR, and makes the adrenal cortex release **aldosterone**, which increases **sodium and water reabsorption**.

questions.solution_md: Renin → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction, aldosterone.

questions.stem_md: State the main functions of the PCT, Henle’s loop and the DCT in urine formation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**PCT:** its brush border reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients and **70–80 percent of electrolytes and water**; it secretes hydrogen ions, ammonia and potassium ions and absorbs bicarbonate.

**Henle’s loop:** maintains the **high osmolarity of the medulla**; the descending limb lets **water** out, the ascending limb lets **electrolytes** out.

**DCT:** **conditional reabsorption** of sodium ions and water; absorbs bicarbonate and secretes hydrogen and potassium ions and ammonia to keep **pH and sodium–potassium balance**.

questions.solution_md: Roles of three segments.

questions.stem_md: How do Henle’s loop and the vasa recta together allow the kidney to produce concentrated urine?

answer.model_answer_md: Filtrate flows in **opposite directions** in the two limbs of Henle’s loop, and blood in the two limbs of the **vasa recta**: **counter-currents**. NaCl leaving the ascending limb passes into the descending vasa recta and is returned to the interstitium by its ascending limb; **urea** cycles between the collecting duct and the ascending limb. This keeps a **gradient of about 300 to 1200 mOsmol per L**, so **water leaves the collecting duct**, concentrating the urine.

questions.solution_md: Counter-currents, NaCl and urea, gradient, water from collecting duct.

marking_scheme.step: Opposite flows in loop and vasa recta
NaCl and urea exchange builds 300–1200 gradient

questions.stem_md: On a cool day a girl drinks two litres of water within an hour; on a hot day she sweats heavily and drinks little. Using the ADH feedback mechanism, explain how her urine differs on the two days.

answer.model_answer_md: On the **hot day**, fluid loss activates **osmoreceptors**, and the **hypothalamus** releases **ADH** from the **neurohypophysis**. ADH increases **water reabsorption** from the later parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis, so she passes **little, concentrated urine**. On the **cool day**, the extra body fluid **switches off the osmoreceptors** and **ADH release is suppressed**, so less water is reabsorbed and she passes **much dilute urine**.

questions.solution_md: ADH high when dehydrated; low after drinking.

marking_scheme.step: Hot day: more water reabsorbed, little concentrated urine
Cool day: ADH suppressed, much dilute urine

questions.stem_md: Describe the formation of urine in a human nephron, explaining glomerular filtration, reabsorption and tubular secretion and the part played by each segment of the tubule.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Filtration.** About 1100–1200 mL of blood reaches the kidneys each minute. Glomerular blood pressure forces fluid through the capillary endothelium, the basement membrane and the epithelium of Bowman’s capsule, whose podocytes leave filtration slits. Everything in plasma except proteins passes: ultrafiltration. The GFR is about 125 mL per minute, 180 litres a day.

**Reabsorption.** Nearly 99 percent of the filtrate is taken back. Glucose, amino acids and sodium ions are reabsorbed actively; nitrogenous wastes and, in the early segments, water passively.

**Secretion.** Tubular cells add hydrogen ions, potassium ions and ammonia to the filtrate, keeping ionic and acid–base balance.

**Segments.** The PCT, with a brush border, reabsorbs nearly all nutrients and 70–80 percent of electrolytes and water, and secretes hydrogen ions, ammonia and potassium ions. In Henle’s loop the descending limb is permeable to water, concentrating the filtrate, and the ascending limb transports electrolytes out but not water, diluting it; the loop keeps the medulla highly concentrated. The DCT carries out conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water and adjusts pH and potassium. The collecting duct reabsorbs large amounts of water to concentrate the urine, passes some urea into the medulla, and secretes hydrogen and potassium ions.

questions.solution_md: Three processes and segment roles.

marking_scheme.step: Roles of PCT, loop, DCT, collecting duct

questions.stem_md: Explain the counter-current mechanism of the mammalian kidney. Why would a person whose Henle’s loops could not transport NaCl out of the ascending limb pass large volumes of dilute urine?

answer.model_answer_md:
**Arrangement.** Henle’s loop dips into the medulla beside the vasa recta. Filtrate flows down the descending limb and up the ascending limb, in opposite directions, forming a counter-current; blood flows the same way in the two limbs of the vasa recta.

**Building the gradient.** The descending limb is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, while the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports NaCl out into the interstitium. This NaCl is taken up by the descending limb of the vasa recta and returned to the interstitium by its ascending limb, so it is not washed away. Small amounts of urea leave the collecting duct, enter the thin ascending limb and are returned to the interstitium by the collecting tubule. Together these keep the medullary osmolarity rising from about 300 mOsmol per L in the cortex to about 1200 in the inner medulla.

**Concentrating urine.** As the collecting duct passes through this increasingly concentrated medulla, water moves out of it, so urine up to nearly four times as concentrated as the filtrate can be formed.

**The patient.** If NaCl could not leave the ascending limb, the medullary gradient would not build up. Without a concentrated interstitium, little water would be drawn out of the collecting duct even when ADH is present, so large volumes of dilute urine would be passed.

questions.solution_md: Counter-current mechanism; prediction.

questions.stem_md: Compare how ADH, the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone mechanism and ANF act on the kidney and on blood pressure. Predict which of them would be most active (i) after heavy sweating on a hot day and (ii) after a large volume of fluid is given rapidly through a drip, giving reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
**ADH.** Excessive loss of fluid stimulates osmoreceptors and the hypothalamus, which releases antidiuretic hormone from the neurohypophysis. ADH increases water reabsorption from the later parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis; it also constricts blood vessels, raising blood pressure and GFR. A rise in body fluid volume switches it off.

**Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone.** A fall in glomerular blood flow, pressure or GFR makes the JG cells release renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and then angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor that raises glomerular pressure and GFR, and it stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which increases reabsorption of sodium ions and water from the distal tubule, raising blood pressure.

**ANF.** Increased blood flow to the atria makes the heart release atrial natriuretic factor, which causes vasodilation and lowers blood pressure, acting as a check on the renin–angiotensin mechanism.

**(i) Heavy sweating.** Body fluid and blood volume fall, so ADH release rises and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone mechanism is activated, conserving water and salt; ANF stays low.

**(ii) Rapid drip.** Blood volume and atrial filling rise, so ANF is released, while ADH and renin are suppressed; more water is lost in urine and blood pressure is brought down.

questions.solution_md: Three regulators compared; two predictions.

questions.stem_md: A 60-year-old man’s blood urea level keeps rising and his doctors say his kidneys are failing. Explain the danger of this condition and describe the two main treatments open to him. Name and define two other disorders of the kidney.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Danger.** When kidneys malfunction, urea accumulates in the blood, a condition called uraemia. It is highly harmful and may lead to kidney failure, in which the body can no longer remove its nitrogenous wastes.

**Haemodialysis.** Blood is drained from a convenient artery and an anticoagulant such as heparin is added. It is pumped into a dialysing unit containing a coiled cellophane tube surrounded by dialysing fluid that has the same composition as plasma except for nitrogenous wastes. The porous membrane allows molecules to pass along their concentration gradient, so urea and other nitrogenous wastes move out of the blood into the fluid. Anti-heparin is added to the cleared blood, which is returned to the body through a vein. Dialysis must be repeated regularly.

**Kidney transplantation.** This is the ultimate method of correcting acute renal failure. A functioning kidney is taken from a donor, preferably a close relative, to minimise the chance of rejection by the patient’s immune system; modern clinical procedures have increased the success rate.

**Other disorders.** Renal calculi are stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts, such as oxalates, formed within the kidney. Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney.

questions.solution_md: Uraemia; dialysis; transplant; two disorders.
